anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical table, index, and partition design does not fit actual access patterns, forcing even well-written SQL to use inherently inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics, often because of cost-model or plan-cache quirks.

Composite definition: Both a static mismatch in the physical schema and a dynamic mis-selection of execution plans coexist. Poor or missing indexes, oversized or redundant structures, and ill-suited partitions leave only a small set of viable access paths, while the optimizer still fails to pick the best among those, compounding inefficiency.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Workload exhibits frequent full table or non-covering index scans, but even when suitable indexes are present the same statements sometimes flip between different bad plans. You may observe extreme variance in response times, sudden CPU or I/O spikes, bloated buffer-pool churn, and lock contention as long-running scans block short OLTP lookups. Adding or modifying an index may help one statement yet unexpectedly slow another because the optimizer latches onto the new structure with an ill-costed plan. Performance improvements gained by manual hinting or index tuning are fragile, disappearing after plan cache invalidations, statistics refreshes, or version upgrades.

Causal interaction: The deficient physical design narrows the pool of efficient plans, increasing the likelihood that any costing inaccuracy or plan-cache quirk will land on a pathological path. Conversely, when the optimizer does stumble upon a partly efficient plan, the absence of covering or selective indexes forces additional key lookups or broad range scans that negate the benefit. Repeated plan flips driven by parameter sensitivity or cache pollution obscure the root schema issue, while the schema flaw magnifies the cost gaps between good and bad plans, making performance instability more severe and harder to diagnose. Together, the two anomalies reinforce each other and degrade both transactional and analytical workloads far beyond the impact each would have in isolation.

entry.official_definition: The number of seconds that the mysqld server waits for a connect packet before responding with Bad handshake.
entry.trigger_condition: A client does not complete the initial connection packet exchange within connect_timeout.
entry.workload_impact: The connection attempt fails during handshake.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
